summary: Defines a way for a mobile node to identify itself by including its Network Access Identifier in the Mobile IP registration request. It also updates RFC 2290 for the Mobile-IPv4 option in IPCP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 2794 gives a mobile node a way to say who it is before it has an address. The Network Access Identifier is the name a dial-up user types to log in, and the extension puts that name into the registration request a mobile node sends when it arrives somewhere new.

Because the name alone identifies the node, the request may leave the Home Address field set to zero and ask for an address instead. The document also relaxes an earlier rule so that the address can be zero during the PPP setup phase, and it defines four error codes for when things go wrong.

subtitle: Letting a mobile node identify itself by name, so it can register without a home address.

tldr.problem: Dial-up networks authenticate their users through AAA servers, which identify a client by the Network Access Identifier it sends. A mobile node arriving in a foreign network had no equivalent, so it could not be recognised until it already had a home address.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2794 defines a Mobile Node NAI extension for the Mobile IP registration request. The extension carries the user's name, and a request that includes it may set the Home Address field to zero to ask for one to be assigned.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from March 2000 that updates RFC 2290 so the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration option to IPCP may carry a zero Home Address. It has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Updates
facts.value: RFC 2290, the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration option for PPP IPCP

today: RFC 2794 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2000. It updates RFC 2290, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The document leaves NAI-based registration for Mobile IPv6 out of scope and offers only ideas for it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
AAA servers are in use within the internet to provide authentication and authorization services for dial-up computers. Such services are likely to be equally valuable for mobile nodes using Mobile IP when the nodes attempt to connect to foreign domains with AAA servers. AAA servers today identify clients by using the Network Access Identifier. This document specifies the Mobile Node NAI extension to the Mobile IP registration request message from the mobile node.

Because the NAI is typically used to uniquely identify the mobile node, the mobile node's home address is not always necessary to provide that function. A mobile node can therefore authenticate itself, and be authorized for connection to the foreign domain, without even having a home address. A message containing the Mobile Node NAI extension may set the Home Address field to zero in the Registration Request, to request that a home address be assigned.

The Mobile-IPv4 Configuration option to IPCP has been specified in RFC 2290 for proper interaction between a mobile node and a peer, through which the mobile node connects to the network using PPP. In that specification the Mobile Node's Home Address field of the option must not be zero. In the context of this document, which allows a mobile node to be identified by its NAI and to obtain an address after the PPP phase of connection establishment, the Home Address field is allowed to be zero while all other aspects of RFC 2290 are maintained.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this document, a mobile node needed a home address before it could say anything useful. The change is to let the node send its name first and ask for the address afterwards.

sections.title: The Mobile Node NAI Extension
sections.content:
The Mobile Node NAI extension contains the user name following the format defined in RFC 2486. When it is present in the Registration Request, the Home Address field may be set to zero. The extension must appear in the Registration Request before both the Mobile-Home Authentication extension and the Mobile-Foreign Authentication extension, if present.

The extension has three fields. The Type is 131 and is skippable. The Length is the length in bytes of the MN-NAI field. The MN-NAI is a string in the NAI format defined in RFC 2486.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is three fields: a type number of 131, a length in bytes, and the name itself as a string. It has to come before the authentication extensions, because the name is what the foreign agent needs in order to check who is asking.

sections.title: Foreign Agent Considerations
sections.content:
If the Home Address is zero in the Registration Request, the foreign agent must use the NAI instead in its pending registration request records, along with the Identification field as usual. If the foreign agent cannot manage pending registration request records in this way, it must return a Registration Reply with a Code indicating NONZERO_HOMEADDR_REQD.

If the mobile node includes the Mobile Node NAI extension in its Registration Request, then the Registration Reply from the home agent must include the Mobile Node NAI extension. If it does not, the foreign agent should send the Registration Reply to the mobile node with the Code changed to MISSING_NAI. The Registration Reply must include a nonzero Home Agent address and a nonzero Home Address for the mobile node. If it does not, the foreign agent should send the Registration Reply to the mobile node with the Code changed to MISSING_HOME_AGENT or MISSING_HOMEADDR respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: The foreign agent keeps its pending records under the name rather than the address when the address is zero. If it cannot work that way, it asks for a real address instead. On the way back, the reply has to carry the extension again and a usable home agent and home address, or the foreign agent rewrites the error code to say which one is missing.

sections.title: Interactions with the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option to IPCP
sections.content:
In the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option to IPCP, the Mobile Node's Home Address field may be zero. The document specifies the action to be taken in that case, when the mobile node is using the Mobile Node NAI extension in the Mobile IP registration request. Whether or not the IP Address Configuration Option contains a nonzero IP address, the mobile node will subsequently attempt to obtain a home address from the Mobile IP registration reply.

If the IP Address Configuration Option to IPCP has an IP address equal to zero, the PPP peer is expected to allocate and assign a co-located care-of address to the mobile node. If, on the other hand, the IP Address Configuration Option to IPCP has a nonzero IP address, the PPP peer is expected to assign that address to the mobile node as its co-located care-of address.

Finally, if the IP Address Configuration Option is left out of the IPCP Configure-Request, then no co-located care-of address is assigned during IPCP. The mobile node will acquire a co-located care-of address during a later stage of configuration, or will use a care-of address located at a foreign agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Three cases during the PPP setup. If the peer offers no address, it is expected to invent one for the node to use while it is away. If the peer offers an address, that address is used. If the option is left out entirely, the node gets nothing during PPP and picks up an address later, or uses one provided by a foreign agent.

sections.title: Error Values
sections.content:
The document defines four codes that a Registration Reply can carry. NONZERO_HOMEADDR_REQD has the value 96 and is first mentioned in section 3. MISSING_NAI has the value 97 and is first mentioned in section 3. MISSING_HOME_AGENT has the value 98 and is first mentioned in section 3. MISSING_HOMEADDR has the value 99 and is first mentioned in section 3.

All four sit in the range 64 to 127, which is the range conventionally associated with rejection by the foreign agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Four error codes cover the ways the exchange can fail: the foreign agent insists on an address, the reply lost the name, the reply lost the home agent address, or the reply lost the home address.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The Mobile Node NAI extension defined in section 2 is a Mobile IP registration extension as defined in RFC 2002 and extended in RFC 2356. IANA should assign a value of 131 for this purpose.

The Code values defined in section 5 are error codes as defined in RFC 2002 and extended in RFC 2344 and RFC 2356. They correspond to error values conventionally associated with rejection by the foreign agent, that is, values from the range 64 to 127. IANA should record the values as defined in section 5.
sections.plainLanguage: Two registry entries are needed: the extension type number and the four error codes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Mobile IP registration messages are authenticated, and the authentication is verified by the recipient. This proposal does not prohibit the mobile node from sending its NAI in the clear over the network, but that is not expected to be a security issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration itself is authenticated, so the name in the extension travels inside an authenticated message. The document does not forbid sending the name in the clear and does not treat that as a problem.

sections.title: IPv6 Considerations
sections.content:
Supporting NAI-based registrations for Mobile IPv6 is outside the scope of this document. The section contains some ideas for how Stateless Address Autoconfiguration and DHCPv6 might be extended to support NAI-based Mobile IPv6 registrations.

For mobile nodes using IPv6, there are no commonly deployed mechanisms by which a mobile node may present its credentials, such as exist today with IPv4. Nevertheless, a mobile node using IPv6 mobility may wish to specify the domain in which its credentials may be checked, by using a NAI just as this specification proposes for IPv4. In the case of IPv6 there is no foreign agent in place to manage the connectivity of the mobile node, and thus to manage the verification of the credentials offered by the mobile node. To identify the Home Domain Allocation Function that has the expected relationship with the mobile node, the NAI would have to be forwarded to a local AAA by the local agent involved with configuring the care-of address of the mobile node.

That agent can either be a router sending Router Advertisements, or a DHCPv6 server. In the former case the router could signal its ability to handle the NAI by attaching some yet to be defined option to the Router Advertisement. In the latter case, for managed links, the mobile node could include a yet to be defined NAI extension in its DHCP Solicitation message, and such an NAI extension and appropriate authentication would also be required on the subsequent DHCP Request sent to the DHCP Server selected on the basis of received DHCP Advertisements. Once a care-of address on the foreign network has been obtained, the mobile node can use regular Mobile IPv6.

The appendix describes the Home Domain Allocation Function, a function that can dynamically assign a home address to the mobile node. It receives messages from foreign agents and assigns a home address within the home domain. It performs no Mobile IP processing on the registration request, but simply forwards the request to a home agent within the network that is able to handle it. On receipt of the registration request from the mobile node, the foreign agent extracts the NAI and finds the domain name associated with it, then finds the function that handles requests for the mobile node's domain. The discovery protocol is outside the scope of the specification, though as an example the foreign agent might delegate the duty of finding the function to a local AAA server, which may also assist in verifying the credentials of the mobile node using protocols not specified in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The same idea for IPv6 is sketched but not specified, because IPv6 mobility has no foreign agent to hold the pending request. The appendix offers a function that assigns a home address and forwards the request to a home agent, but how a foreign agent finds that function is left open.

messages.label: Registration Request
messages.note: Carries the Mobile Node NAI extension. The Home Address field may be set to zero.

messages.label: Registration Request
messages.note: The pending registration request record is kept under the NAI, because the Home Address is zero.

messages.label: Registration Reply
messages.note: Must include the Mobile Node NAI extension, a nonzero Home Agent address and a nonzero Home Address.

messages.label: Registration Reply
messages.note: The foreign agent rewrites the Code if the reply is missing the extension or either address.

viz.caption: What happens during PPP setup in each case

items.title: The option carries zero
items.text: The PPP peer is expected to allocate and assign a co-located care-of address to the mobile node.

items.title: The option carries an address
items.text: The PPP peer is expected to assign that address to the mobile node as its co-located care-of address.

items.title: The option is absent
items.text: No co-located care-of address is assigned during IPCP. The node acquires one later, or uses a care-of address located at a foreign agent.

items.label: NONZERO_HOMEADDR_REQD
items.desc: The foreign agent cannot keep pending registration records under the NAI and asks for a nonzero home address.

items.label: MISSING_NAI
items.desc: The Registration Reply from the home agent did not include the Mobile Node NAI extension.

items.label: MISSING_HOME_AGENT
items.desc: The Registration Reply did not include a nonzero Home Agent address.

items.label: MISSING_HOMEADDR
items.desc: The Registration Reply did not include a nonzero Home Address for the mobile node.
